questions.q: What comparison do the authors use to describe how a relationship should be maintained?
a: A regular gym routine that requires steady effort
A garden that only needs attention in spring
A business that grows through careful planning
A journey that becomes easier over time
questions.why: Lesson 1 compares marriage to working out: show up consistently and keep improving weak areas.

questions.q: What do the four letters of the SNAP method stand for?
a: Start strong, no exceptions, always act, practice the will
Slow down, notice feelings, apologize often, pause daily
Speak kindly, negotiate fairly, accept flaws, plan ahead
Stay present, nurture trust, allow space, pursue growth
questions.why: Lesson 2 introduces SNAP as start strong, no exceptions, always act and practice exercising the will.

questions.q: What does the SNAP principle of having no exceptions require?
a: Taking no days off from the commitment you made
Avoiding any disagreement with your partner
Making every decision together as a couple
Refusing to change plans once they are set
questions.why: Lesson 2 says exceptions and small treats tend to break focus, so the habit should continue without days off.

questions.q: Why do the authors suggest taking the VIA survey with your partner?
a: To learn each other's strengths and needs better
To measure how compatible your personalities are
To decide who should handle which household tasks
To track how the relationship changes over time
questions.why: Lesson 3 says the survey reveals strengths, traits and love languages, making it easier to meet each other's needs.

questions.q: What does eudaimonia mean in the summary's discussion of Aristotelian love?
a: A state of flourishing, contentment and joy
A feeling of intense romantic desire
A bond based mainly on shared duties
A life entirely free from conflict
questions.why: Lesson 3 defines eudaimonia as good spirit, describing blessedness, good fortune, contentment and joy.
